content.prompt: Part 1 — The unexpected offer
content.answer: Patol Babu, a fifty-two-year-old man whose stage-acting days were far behind him, was about to go to the market when his neighbour Nishikanto Babu called out. Nishikanto's brother-in-law, Naresh Dutt, who worked in the film business, needed a short, bald-headed man of about fifty for a small role, and Nishikanto had recommended Patol. The offer was beyond Patol Babu's wildest dreams — a chance to act again. In his excitement he bought red chillies instead of onion seeds and quite forgot the aubergines his wife had asked for.

content.prompt: Part 2 — The man who was a star once
content.answer: Long ago, Patol Babu had been in demand in Jatras and amateur theatricals, with his name on handbills and people buying tickets to see him. Life had not treated him kindly since: a job in a railway factory at Kanchrapara, then nine years as a clerk with Hudson and Kimberley in Calcutta, where he lost his post when the war brought retrenchment. A variety store, a Bengali firm, a spell as an insurance agent — nothing had lasted. Now, at the age of fifty-two, he was being offered a film role, and his heart thumped as he went to meet Naresh Dutt, who greeted him at the office gate, mistaking his name for "Atul Babu".

content.prompt: Part 3 — The single word "Oh!"
content.answer: The role was a street scene: Patol Babu was to play an absent-minded pedestrian who collides with the hero, Chanchal Kumar, and must say a single word — "Oh!". When Jyoti handed him a torn page with "Oh" written on it, Patol Babu's heart sank; he felt demeaned. But then he remembered his mentor Gogon Pakrashi's advice — that no role is too small for a true artist, and that every word is like a fruit on a tree, to be plucked and served to the audience. Patol Babu rehearsed the exclamation in a dozen inflections until he discovered that one word could carry many shades of meaning. He even suggested carrying a newspaper, to make the absent-minded pedestrian look natural.

content.prompt: Part 4 — A perfect performance, and no money
content.answer: When the scene was shot, the hero's head knocked hard against Patol Babu's forehead and the pain was intense, but by a supreme effort of will he pulled himself together and cried "Oh!" — mixing fifty parts of anguish, twenty-five of surprise and twenty-five of irritation — and resumed his walk. "Cut!" cried the director. Patol Babu had done the role perfectly. He thought of the small fee — ten, fifteen or twenty rupees — and decided it was nothing compared with the satisfaction of a job done with perfection and dedication. He left the set without taking his money. His mentor Gogon Pakrashi, he was sure, would have been proud of him.

content.prompt: No role is too small — the dignity of work
content.answer: The story's central theme is that the value of a task lies in how it is done, not in its size. Patol Babu is offered a role with a single word of dialogue, yet he treats it with the seriousness of a major part, rehearsing the one word until it carries the whole weight of his craft. The lesson, taught by his mentor Gogon Pakrashi, is that every role, every task, deserves an artist's full attention — for a play, like life, is the combined effort of many.

content.prompt: Artistic satisfaction over money
content.answer: Patol Babu, who badly needs money, chooses satisfaction over payment. After delivering his "Oh!" to perfection, he reflects that the twenty rupees or so he might earn are nothing against the intense satisfaction of a small job done with dedication. He leaves the set without taking his fee. The theme celebrates the true artist's priority: creation and self-respect over reward. Money, the story suggests, can never buy the pride of work perfectly done.

content.prompt: The commercialization of art
content.answer: The story contrasts the film industry's indifference with the artist's devotion. The film unit hires extras for ten or twenty rupees, makes them "go through certain motions", pays them and forgets them. Patol Babu, however, brings to his tiny role a lifetime of craft, and he is hurt by the crew's inability to appreciate what he has given. The theme criticises an age in which art is treated as a commodity, and celebrates the amateur's passion that survives even in a hired extra on a film set.

content.prompt: Patol Babu
content.answer: Patol Babu, whose real name is Sitalakanta Ray, is a fifty-two-year-old former stage actor, now a struggling middle-aged man who once had a real passion — verging on obsession — for the stage. He had been in demand in Jatras and amateur plays, but lost his railway factory job, spent nine years as a clerk at Hudson and Kimberley, and then drifted through a variety store, a Bengali firm and insurance work. He is modest, meticulous and principled: he treats the single word "Oh!" as a masterpiece of interpretation, and refuses payment because he values the satisfaction of perfect work. He is an artist in an age that has forgotten what artists are.

content.prompt: Gogon Pakrashi
content.answer: Gogon Pakrashi was Patol Babu's mentor in his stage days — a wonderful actor without a trace of vanity, a saintly person and an actor in a million. His advice shapes the story: never consider any role beneath your dignity; make the most of every opportunity; and remember that each word an actor speaks is like a fruit on a tree — not everyone in the audience can reach it, but the actor must pluck it, get at its essence and serve it up for their edification. It is his voice that saves Patol Babu from despair and turns the one-word role into a triumph.

content.prompt: Naresh Dutt
content.answer: Naresh Dutt is Nishikanto Babu's brother-in-law, a man of about thirty working in the film business. It is he who was looking for a short, bald-headed man of about fifty for a small part in a street scene, and through Nishikanto he brings the offer to Patol Babu. He is brisk and businesslike, mistaking Patol's name for "Atul Babu" at their first meeting, but he conducts the actor to the set and arranges the shooting. He represents the film industry — efficient, impersonal, and blind to the artistic depths of the extras it hires.

content.prompt: The film unit (the director and crew)
content.answer: The film unit that shoots the street scene treats its extras as numbers: men are hired to perform a few motions, paid ten or twenty rupees, and forgotten. The director, Baren Mullick, calls "Cut!" and praises Patol briefly ("Jolly good!") before turning back to his business, while Sosanko and Jyoti handle the small logistics of the scene. The unit is not cruel — merely indifferent. It provides the story's contrast: the world measures work by the rupee, while the true artist measures it by the heart he pours into it.

content.prompt: Give your best to every task, however small
content.answer: The story teaches that greatness lies in attention to detail. Patol Babu is offered a one-word role and could easily have shrugged it off as beneath him; instead he rehearses "Oh!" in a dozen inflections until it becomes a perfect, shaded performance. The value lesson, from Gogon Pakrashi, is that no task is too small to be done with full dedication — the quality of a life is the sum of the small things done well.

content.prompt: Self-respect is worth more than money
content.answer: Patol Babu needs money badly, yet he walks away from the fee because he will not cheapen the work he has done with love. The lesson: money measures labour, but only self-respect measures the worker. A person who values his own craft will not sell it cheap, even when he is poor; and the satisfaction of work perfectly performed is a reward no payment can match.

content.prompt: Describe Patol Babu's early life and career. How had his fortunes declined?
content.answer: Patol Babu's real name was Sitalakanta Ray, and in his youth he had a passion for the stage that verged on obsession. In Jatras, in amateur theatricals and in plays put up by the club in his neighbourhood, he was always in demand; his name appeared in handbills on countless occasions, once in bold type near the top — "Sitalakanta Ray (Patol Babu) in the role of Parasar" — and people bought tickets especially to see him. He lived then in Kanchrapara, with a job in the railway factory there. In 1934 he was offered higher pay in a clerical post with Hudson and Kimberley in Calcutta, and he gave up the factory job and moved to the city. For a while all went well, but in 1943 the Second World War brought retrenchment and he lost his post after nine years of service. From then on fortune left him: a variety store that lasted five years, a Bengali firm, a spell as an insurance agent — nothing lasted. Now, at fifty-two, he was a nobody, a man who had once been a star and was now lucky to hear a kind word from his neighbour.

content.prompt: How did Patol Babu prepare for his single-word role?
content.answer: When Patol Babu first saw his "dialogue" — the word "Oh" written on a torn page by Jyoti — he was crestfallen; the role seemed an insult to his craft. But as he sat dejected, the memory of Gogon Pakrashi stirred: "However small a part you're offered, never consider it beneath your dignity to accept it. As an artist your aim should be to make the most of your opportunity, and squeeze the last drop of meaning out of your lines." His mentor had also taught him that each word an actor speaks is like a fruit on a tree, to be plucked and served to the audience. Patol Babu began to rehearse, uttering "Oh" over and over with a different inflection each time, and made an astonishing discovery: the same exclamation, spoken in different ways, carried different shades of meaning — surprise, pain, irritation, even humour. He imagined the scene, the impact of the collision, the feelings of the pedestrian. He even suggested to the unit that he should be carrying a newspaper, so the absent-minded pedestrian would look entirely natural. By the time the camera rolled, the one-word role had become a small masterpiece of preparation.

content.prompt: Describe the shooting of the scene and Patol Babu's performance.
content.answer: The scene was a street scene: the hero, Chanchal Kumar, walks along the footpath while Patol Babu, an absent-minded pedestrian with a newspaper, comes the other way. At the signal, the two collided — and the hero's head struck Patol Babu's forehead with such force that the pain was intense and Patol Babu almost lost consciousness. But by a supreme effort of will he pulled himself together. Mixing fifty parts of anguish with twenty-five of surprise and twenty-five of irritation, he cried "Oh!" — exactly as he had rehearsed — and, after a brief pause, resumed his walk as if nothing had happened. "Cut!" shouted the director, and the scene was over. Patol Babu stepped towards the director anxiously asking, "Was that right?" and received a hearty "Jolly good! You're quite an actor." For Patol Babu, that moment was everything: he had taken the humblest role in the film — a collision, one word — and turned it into a piece of true acting, with his mentor Gogon Pakrashi's words ringing in his ears.

content.prompt: Why did Patol Babu refuse to take the money?
content.answer: After the scene, Patol Babu had time to think. He knew the film unit's ways: they got hold of some people, got them to go through certain motions, paid them for their labours and forgot all about it. Paid them, yes — but how much? Ten, fifteen, twenty rupees. He needed money very badly; his circumstances had never been worse. But as he stood there, he measured the sum against what he had just done — a single shot in which he had poured all the labour and imagination of his years on the stage, and had produced, for one instant, the perfect piece of acting his mentor would have blessed. What was twenty rupees against the intense satisfaction of a small job done with perfection and dedication? The money, he felt, would cheapen the achievement; taking it would be like saying his "Oh!" was worth no more than that. So he declined the payment and left the set quietly — poorer in his pocket, but rich in the one thing no one could pay for: the knowledge that he had done his craft honour, and that Gogon Pakrashi, wherever he was, would have been proud of him.

content.prompt: Value question: What does the story teach us about attitude towards work?
content.answer: The story teaches that the worth of our work is determined not by its size but by the heart we bring to it. Patol Babu could have treated his one-word role with contempt — he was, after all, a man who had once been a star. Instead he remembered his mentor's teaching: no role is beneath an artist's dignity; every opportunity deserves the maximum effort; every word is a fruit to be plucked and served. So he rehearsed, refined and perfected a single exclamation until it contained fifty parts of anguish, twenty-five of surprise and twenty-five of irritation. The values the story holds up are dedication, self-respect and the joy of honest craft: work done with love is its own reward, and no amount of money can buy the satisfaction of a job perfectly done. In a world that measures work by wages, the story stands as a quiet reminder that the labourer's true wage is his own pride — and that the small tasks, done supremely well, are what make a life and an art.
